analysis.investment_thesis: Indo Count scores poorly on both Magic Formula metrics — earnings yield of ~7.9% (EBIT ₹535 Cr / EV ~₹6,806 Cr) falls well below my 12% threshold, and ROCE of 13.5% is far short of the 20%+ I require for a "good" business. A capital-heavy, cyclical textile exporter with rising debt and erratic free cash flow does not deserve a P/E of 48x.
key_strengths: Revenue scaling steadily — 8.1% CAGR over 9 years reaching ₹4,151 Cr in FY25, with genuine US bedding market presence
Promoter holding of 58.74% aligns management interests, and rising FII/DII interest signals institutional awareness
Gross margin of 52.4% is respectable for textiles, suggesting some brand/product differentiation in home bedding
key_risks: Debt explosion: borrowings surged from ₹349 Cr (FY20) to ₹1,243 Cr (FY25), dragging finance costs from ₹28 Cr to ₹123 Cr — a 4.4x increase that ate FY25 net profit (₹246 Cr vs ₹338 Cr in FY24)
Erratic free cash flow — FCF positive in only 3 of last 5 years; FY22 FCF was -₹489 Cr; heavy capex cycle (₹252 Cr in FY25) continues to strain cash generation
Net profit CAGR of -0.2% over 9 years: despite doubling revenue since 2016, bottom-line is flat — a hallmark of a low-ROIC commodity business with no pricing power
red_flags: Earnings yield ~7.9% — well below Magic Formula's 12% minimum; stock is not cheap enough for its quality
ROCE of 13.5% and ROE of 11.3% — both below cost of equity; the business is not earning excess returns on capital
Finance costs quadrupled in 4 years while net profit declined — leverage is amplifying risk, not returns
P/E of 48x on a cyclical textile manufacturer with no earnings growth over a decade is a valuation trap
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on Indo Count: EBIT (Operating Income) FY25 = ₹535 Cr. Enterprise Value = Market Cap ₹5,463 Cr + Net Debt ₹1,343 Cr ≈ ₹6,806 Cr. Earnings Yield = 7.9% — not cheap enough. Return on Capital (ROCE) = 13.5% — not a good-enough business. The Magic Formula demands BOTH metrics to be high simultaneously. Indo Count is mediocre on both, earning it a rank near the bottom of any screened universe. The EV/EBITDA of 18.3x is expensive for a cyclical exporter dependent on US demand, USD/INR rates, and cotton input costs.

The deeper problem is capital destruction: the company deployed massive capex (₹452 Cr in FY22, ₹342 Cr in FY23) financed by debt, yet net profit in FY25 (₹246 Cr) is below FY16 levels (₹251 Cr) on twice the revenue. That is the signature of a business with no durable competitive advantage — every rupee reinvested earns sub-par returns. Rising finance costs (₹123 Cr in FY25 vs ₹28 Cr in FY21) are now a structural drag. Unless ROIC can sustainably clear 20%+ and the balance sheet is deleveraged, this fails the Magic Formula screen decisively.
